Right
rīt
adj. & n. (straight, upright, conformed to a rule; also the right hand as the place of power; rendering Hebrew yashar, yamin, Greek orthos, dexios)
From Saxon riht, straight, direct, akin to Latin rectus. The root idea is a straight line, and every moral use of the word depends on there being a rule straight enough to measure by.

Biblical Definition

Right in the Authorized Version runs along two lines that meet in Christ. The first is position: the right hand is the place of strength and honour, and the Father assigns it to the Son. “The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool” (Psalm 110:1) — the verse the New Testament quotes more than any other, and Hebrews reports its fulfilment: when He “had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high” (Hebrews 1:3). The second line is moral: right is what conforms to God's rule, and Scripture is blunt that the creature is not a competent judge of it. The book of Judges closes on the sentence that explains the whole ruin: “In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25). Proverbs generalizes it into a warning about sincerity: “There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death” (Proverbs 14:12). Note what is conceded. The way seems right; the man is not lying, he is deceived, and the error is fatal anyway. So the two lines converge: because there is a King at the right hand, there is a rule that is right apart from my eyes — and my eyes are exactly the instrument Scripture says has failed.

Webster 1828 Definition

Straight, and hence conformed to the standard of truth and justice; also the right hand, the side of power and honour. Judges 21:25 and Proverbs 14:12 both name the same failure — a man judging right by his own eyes.

expand to see more

RIGHT, a. [Sax. riht; L. rectus; from the root of rego, to rule, to make straight.] Properly, strait; direct; not crooked; as a right line.

2. Conformable to the will of God, or to his law; just; equitable; not deviating from the standard of moral rectitude. That which is right is holy and good.

3. Conformable to truth; not erroneous; correct in judgment or opinion.

4. Fit; suitable; proper; becoming; as the right man for the office.

5. Denoting the side opposite to the left, and by figure the side of honor and power. Sit thou at my right hand. Ps. 110.

Key Scripture

Psalm 110:1 — "A Psalm of David. The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool."

Judges 21:25 — "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes."

Proverbs 14:12 — "There is a way which seemeth right unto a man, but the end thereof are the ways of death."

Hebrews 1:3 — "Who being the brightness of his glory, and the express image of his person, and upholding all things by the word of his power, when he had by himself purged our sins, sat down on the right hand of the Majesty on high;"

Modern Corruption

The word has migrated from right as a standard outside the man to rights as a claim asserted by him — and once the plural noun swallows the adjective, Judges 21:25 stops reading as an indictment and starts reading as a description of freedom.

expand to see more

Two moves accomplish this, and they are usually made without argument. The first replaces conformity to a rule with authenticity to a self: what is right for a man becomes whatever is genuinely his, and the highest sin becomes insincerity rather than transgression. The second turns the moral vocabulary into the language of entitlement, so that public debate is a collision of asserted rights with no standard above them by which any could be adjudicated. Scripture anticipated both. Judges 21:25 is a verdict, not a charter, and the book has just spent five chapters showing what every man doing right in his own eyes actually produces — a mutilated concubine, a civil war, and abducted daughters. Proverbs 14:12 forecloses the appeal to sincerity in advance: the way seemeth right, and the man walking it is not a hypocrite. He is sincere and he is going to die.

The recovery runs through the other sense of the word. There is a right hand, and it is occupied. Psalm 110:1 says a King sits there until His enemies are made His footstool, and Hebrews 1:3 says He sat down because the purging of sins was finished. That is the ground on which the moral sense of right can be held without tyranny: the rule is not an abstraction that crushes, but the will of a King who bled to bring rebels under it. Where that throne is denied, the only available standard is the individual eye, and the culture that results is not free but arbitrary, since a claim asserted can always be out-asserted. Where the throne is confessed, a man may be told he is wrong and live — because the One who tells him has already sat down.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yashar (straight, upright, right), yamin (the right hand), and tsedeq (righteousness as conformity to a standard); Greek orthos (straight), dexios (the right hand), dikaios (just, right).

expand to see more

Hebrew yashar (H3477) — straight, upright, right; the word in “right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25) and in doing that which is right in the sight of the LORD.

Hebrew yamin (H3225) — the right hand, the side of strength; the term in Psalm 110:1.

Hebrew tsedeq (H6664) — rightness, justice, righteousness; the standard by which a way is judged right rather than merely felt to be.

Greek dexios (G1188) — right, right hand; used of the Son seated at the right hand of the Majesty (Hebrews 1:3).

Greek orthos (G3717) — straight, erect; the root behind orthotomeo, to divide rightly, in 2 Timothy 2:15.

Usage

"“Sit thou at my right hand” — the place of power given, not seized."

"“Every man did that which was right in his own eyes” — the closing verdict of Judges, not a description of liberty."

"“There is a way which seemeth right unto a man” — sincerity conceded, and the end still death."
